newsitem.title: USA: Simpson weary after two long days on witness stand.
newsitem.headline: Simpson weary after two long days on witness stand.

text.p: In two grueling days on the witness stand in his civil trial, O.J. Simpson has felt the brunt of his accusers' attack as they have tried to undermine his credibility and shoot holes in his alibi.
But with the former football star facing one more day of testimony on Tuesday before the start of a long Thanksgiving holiday recess, his attorneys may have a chance to undo some of the damage.
Simpson is expected to finish his current testimony on Tuesday, but is likely to be recalled to the stand by Baker during the defence phase of the trial.
Simpson was acquitted last October of murdering his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ron Goldman. He is now battling a wrongful death lawsuit by the victims' families.
Simpson appeared drained at the end of Monday's dramatic session, as lead plaintiffs' attorney Daniel Petrocelli lashed into him with a series of accusations.
"You know you committed those murders," Petrocelli said. "You went there (Nicole Brown Simpson's townhouse) that night and you confronted her and you killed her. True?" Petrocelli asked.
"That's totally, absolutely incorrect," Simpson shot back.
"And Ron Goldman came upon you when you were there with Nicole and you didn't expect him," Petrocelli continued, his voice getting louder. "Untrue," Simpson said.
"Ron Goldman got in a fight with you and you cut him and you sliced him until he died and collapsed in your arms," Petrocelli persisted. "Untrue," Simpson said.
Finishing with a flourish, Petrocelli went on, "And you left him to die with his eyes wide open looking right at you. True or not?"
"That's untrue," Simpson responded wearily, and Petrocelli said he had no further questions.
During the exchange Sharon Rufo, Goldman's natural mother, and his sister, Kim, were crying. Goldman's father, Fred, and his stepmother, Patti, held hands tightly.
Earlier on Monday Simpson admitted he was contemplating suicide during the now-famous Bronco chase, saying he was "in a lot of pain" over his wife's death at the time.
But he repeatedly denied owning the brown leather gloves and size 12 Bruno Magli shoes that lawyers for the victims maintain the killer wore.
Simpson said he owned many pairs of leather gloves in several different colours, and had no idea if any of them were the Aris Leather Lights used by the killer.
Shown a picture of himself at a 1993 football game in Buffalo wearing shoes that an FBI expert has identified as the Bruno Maglis, Simpson insisted the photograph had been doctored.
"My opinion is that it is a fraud," he said.
Petrocelli was blistering in his two days of questioning Simpson, often cutting off his witness in mid-sentence to launch another salvo or jabbing an accusatory finger toward him.

But Simpson's lawyer, Robert Baker, could get the chance to examine his client before the Thanksgiving break, no doubt using a gentler approach to advance the defence theory that police officers framed Simpson for the murders.

Loyola University Law School professor Laurie Levenson said Simpson has probably scored points with his matter-of-fact answers to often hostile questions, but noted that appearances could fail him in the jury room.

"He got up there and in a very calm and collected manner said everybody else and all the other witnesses were wrong," Levenson said. "His demeanor is fine but the problem is he's contradicting everything ... and that will be hard for the jury to accept."

An alternate juror was to be appointed to the permanent panel on Tuesday following the dismissal of a female juror by Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki at the end of Monday's session. It was not immediately known why the juror was dismissed.
